Choosing Motorcycle Luggage for Touring

The right luggage system transforms your motorcycle from a fun road machine into a capable touring platform. But with dozens of options from hard panniers to dry bags, choosing the right setup for UK touring can be bewildering. Here's how to decide.

Types of Motorcycle Luggage

Hard Panniers

Rigid boxes mounted on a frame system. Brands include Givi, SW-Motech, and OEM options.

  • Pros: Waterproof, lockable, crash-resistant, hold their shape. Best security for leaving gear on the bike.
  • Cons: Expensive (£400-1000+ with frames), add width to the bike (challenging on narrow lanes), heavy when empty, require a mounting frame.
  • Best for: Long tours, riders who value security and weatherproofing, adventure bikes with wide handlebars.

Soft Panniers

Textile or nylon bags that strap or clip to the bike. Brands include Kriega, SW-Motech, Enduristan.

  • Pros: Lighter than hard panniers, flexible (won't crack in a tip-over), more forgiving on narrow UK lanes, easier to store off the bike.
  • Cons: Not fully waterproof (need rain covers or dry bags inside), can't be locked to the bike, less structured so packing is fussier.
  • Best for: Lightweight touring, narrower bikes, riders who want flexibility.

Tank Bags

  • Magnetic mount: Easy on/off, works on steel tanks. Not suitable for aluminium or plastic tanks.
  • Strap mount: Universal fit, stays put on any tank material.
  • Ring-lock mount: Quick-release systems (Givi, SW-Motech) that clip to a ring on the fuel cap. Very secure.
  • Best for: Daily essentials — phone, wallet, snacks, map, camera. The most-used piece of touring luggage.

Tail Bags and Dry Bags

  • Sit on the pillion seat, secured with straps or a rack.
  • Capacity from 10L to 60L+. A 30-40L dry bag covers most weekend-to-week touring needs.
  • Dry bags (roll-top closure) are inherently waterproof — a huge advantage in UK conditions.
  • Can replace panniers entirely for minimalist tourers.
For UK touring, waterproofing is non-negotiable. Whatever luggage you choose, assume it will get rained on. If the bags aren't waterproof, pack everything inside dry bags or zip-lock bags within them. There's nothing worse than arriving at camp with soaking clothes.

How Much Capacity Do You Need?

  • Day ride: Tank bag only (5-15L)
  • Weekend (2 days, hotels): Tank bag + small tail bag (30-40L total)
  • Weekend (2 days, camping): Tank bag + tail bag + small panniers (50-70L total)
  • Week tour (hotels): Tank bag + panniers or large tail bag (60-80L total)
  • Week tour (camping): Tank bag + panniers + tail bag (80-120L total)

Weight Distribution

How you load your luggage affects handling as much as what you carry:

  • Heavy items go low and close to the bike's centre of gravity
  • Balance weight equally between left and right panniers
  • Don't overload the tail — a top-heavy rear makes the bike unstable
  • Tank bags shouldn't impede steering lock or block instrument visibility
  • Test-ride your loaded bike around the block before committing to a tour

Our Recommendation for UK Touring

For most UK touring, the ideal setup is:

  • A medium tank bag (10-15L) for daily essentials
  • Soft panniers (20-30L each) for clothing and gear
  • A waterproof tail bag (20-30L) for camping kit or overflow

This gives you 70-100L of capacity with good weight distribution, and it all comes off the bike easily when you stop for the night. Start with what you have, test it, and upgrade as you discover your needs.
keyTakeaways: The main options are hard panniers, soft panniers, tank bags and tail/dry bags.
Hard panniers are secure and waterproof but expensive and wide; soft panniers are lighter, cheaper and more forgiving.
Tank bags mount magnetically, by strap or ring-lock and hold daily essentials.
A week camping needs roughly 80-100 litres total capacity; a hotel weekend far less.
Keep heavy items low and central and balance pannier weight for stable handling.

faq.q: Hard or soft panniers for UK touring?
faq.a: Hard panniers are lockable, fully waterproof and protect their contents, which suits Scottish Highland weather and cafe stops, but they are expensive and stick out wide, catching hedges on Cornish lanes. Soft panniers such as quality Kriega bags are lighter, cheaper, more flexible and easier to squeeze through tight spaces, though they offer less security when parked. Many UK riders favour soft luggage for narrow lanes.

faq.q: How much luggage capacity do I need?
faq.a: Match capacity to the trip. A day ride needs just a 5-15L tank bag; a hotel weekend around 30-40L; a camping weekend 50-70L; a week in hotels 60-80L; and a week camping the full 80-100L across panniers, a tail pack and a tank bag. Resist over-buying, as excess space simply encourages you to carry more weight than you need.

faq.q: How should I distribute luggage weight?
faq.a: Keep heavy items low and close to the bike's centre of gravity, and balance the two panniers so they weigh roughly the same. Avoid putting anything heavy in a high tail pack, as it raises the centre of gravity and makes the bike feel top-heavy and unstable. Pack tools and boots in the panniers and lighter, bulky clothes higher up.

faq.q: What tank bag mount should I choose?
faq.a: Magnetic tank bags are quick to fit but only work on steel tanks and can shift at speed. Strap-mounted bags suit plastic or non-magnetic tanks. Ring-lock systems, which clip to a fitted ring around the filler cap, are the most secure and stable option and are ideal for a bag you use on every tour. Whichever you choose, make sure it does not obscure the filler cap.
